To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
AGS is an encephalopathy characterized by an IFN‐dependent gene signature.
the gene‐expression profile of AGS cases is characterized by upregulation of IFN‐related genes and downregulation of angiopoietin‐1 and cystatin F.
the interferon‐related transcriptome alterations in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid cells of Aicardi– Goutières syndrome patients are consistent with the clinical course of the disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of gene expression in CSF cells of AGS patients.
the identification of the gene‐expression signature in AGS patients and its possible use in the development of new therapeutic approaches.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the IFN‐related encephalo‐lymphadenopathy of AGS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IFN‐alpha exposure in AGS is a cause of the disease and that the IFN‐dependent gene‐expression pattern is the result of IFN‐alpha‐induced damage.
AGS is an autoimmune disease with an IFN‐related pathogenetic mechanism.
the IFN‐related transcriptome alterations in the cerebrospinal fluids of AGS patients may reflect an ongoing IFN‐mediated neuroinflammation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IFN‐alpha exposure during the first years of life induces a gene‐expression signature in the CSF lymphocyte compartment, which may be responsible for the clinical features observed in AGS patients.

IFN‐dependent gene‐expression signature in AGS patients is characterized by the activation of genes involved in lymphocytic activation and IFN‐dependent pathway, paralleled by a downregulation of angiopoietic genes, and a progressive age‐dependent increase in the expression of genes with a negative feedback on the IFN‐dependent signalling pathway.

the CSF cells of AGS patients are exposed to IFN‐α and that this interferon‐related environment is associated with a gene‐expression signature that is characterized by upregulation of IFN‐dependent genes and lymphocyte functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CSF lymphocyte transcriptome of AGS patients is characterized by a gene‐expression signature that is consistent with the activation of the IFN system and with the impairment of angiopoietic pathways, which is consistent with the clinical picture of AGS.
AGS is characterized by an IFN‐dependent transcriptome signature that is progressively attenuated with age.
IFN‐related transcriptome alterations in CSF cells of AGS patients may provide a new insight for understanding the pathogenesis of this rare syndrome.
